scenarios.name: Deal: each seat gets 3 cards, 16 stay in deck (after one trick each hand holds 2)
Each player holds their own dealt hand (hand sizes only, deal is random)
All seats bid 0-3 and the bids are recorded
Hand 2 is led by seat 2 (all-Escape deal, so the leader wins the trick)
Play goes clockwise from the leader: the first Pirate (seat 1, after leader 3) wins
A suited card played after an Escape sets the lead suit, so seat 3 must follow Yellow
No suited card played: no lead suit, the Mermaid wins
Holding the lead suit, seat 2 is offered only Green and special cards
The leader and a player void in the lead suit are offered every card
Mermaid beats the Skull King
Skull King beats a Pirate when there is no Mermaid
The first Pirate played wins
Mermaid wins without Skull King or Pirate
The highest Black card wins over the lead suit
The highest card of the lead suit wins and an off-suit card does not
All Escapes: the first card played (the leader, seat 2) wins
The trick winner gains a trick and leads the next trick (shown by the all-Escape last trick)
Skull King capturing two Pirates adds 60 bonus, paid on an exact bid
Mermaid capturing the Skull King adds 40 bonus
After a trick the winner is recorded for everyone (tricks_won)
An exact bid of 2 scores +40 and an exact bid of 1 scores +20
Bid 0 and won 0 scores +20
Bid 0 but won a trick scores -20 and loses the Skull King bonus
A missed bid scores -10 per trick of difference and loses the bonus
At the end of a hand scores are applied and tricks_won resets to 0
The game ends after round 27 is scored; the highest score wins
Seats tied for the highest final score share the win

spec_choices.why: The designer fixed the game at 3 seats, and the 25-card deck, the 3-card deal and the clockwise leader rotation are all built for 3. Minimum and maximum are both 3.

spec_choices.what: No free-talk step before bids or plays
spec_choices.why: The source has no talk. Strategy comes from reading the revealed bids and the cards played (whether to win or duck a trick to land your own bid, or to spoil a rival's), so added talk would only add words.

spec_choices.what: One trick per round, with the deal, bid and scoring steps run only when trick_in_hand is 1 or 3
spec_choices.why: The source sets each round to one trick (27 rounds). Single-step 'when' conditions keep the step list flat.

spec_choices.what: Ties at the top share the win
spec_choices.why: The source calls a top tie a draw among the tied players, which is exactly a shared win.

simplifications.what: The 16 undealt cards stay in the deck list rather than a separate set-aside pile
simplifications.why: They are unseen and unused until the next hand's reshuffle, so a separate list adds nothing.

simplifications.what: Card play uses ask in seat order starting from the leader
simplifications.why: Tricks are sequential in the source; each later player must see the earlier cards to follow suit.

variation.original_summary: Skull King is a 2-8 player trick-taking game played over 10 hands of growing size. In each hand players bid simultaneously on exactly how many tricks they will win, then play tricks that include special cards (Pirates, Escapes, Mermaids, the Skull King). They score heavily for an exact bid and lose points for a miss.

review.evidence: No fixed bid survives. Always bidding 0 and dumping low cards fails whenever a player is forced to win a trick, which costs hand-number x 10 and up to 100 in hand 10. Always bidding high rarely comes in exact. The deal and lead rotate, so there is little seat edge. One weakness is the zero bid: it pays hand x 10 regardless of hand size, so it is lopsided in late hands.

Reading your hand, adjusting play to land exactly on your bid, and playing to make opponents miss theirs all separate strong players from weak ones over 10 hands. The deal matters for bonuses (who holds the Skull King or a Mermaid), but the exact-bid rule rewards judgement whatever the cards.
Card counting, inference from public bids, deliberately setting opponents, and endgame risk-taking when trailing give a deep skill ceiling. A beginner still scores by bidding conservatively.
Hands are hidden and bids are public signals. Players must infer what others hold from their bids and earlier plays, and plan the order of their own cards across a hand.
Trick winners and scores follow mechanically from the cards played and the bids.

It is text-only and arithmetic, but too large to build. Hands grow to 10 cards, a full game runs 55 tricks per player, the deck has 70 cards, up to 8 players each act per trick (more than 4 choice steps), and Scary Mary adds a declaration choice. All of this must be compressed.

problems: Too long and too large: 10 hands of growing size means 55 tricks, and with up to 8 players each trick needs more than the 4 choice steps allowed per round.
The 70-card deck with many special cards inflates the dealing and resolution steps beyond what the engine builds reliably.
Scary Mary needs an extra declaration choice when played, which adds a choice step for little strategic value.
The zero-bid payoff (hand number x 10) grows with hand number rather than with difficulty, which distorts late-hand bidding.
With growing hand sizes and an uneven count of hands per seat, the first-leader seat is not equalised.

changes.what: Fix the game at 3 players, every hand 3 cards, 9 hands, so each round of the engine is one trick (27 rounds).
changes.why: One trick per round needs at most 4 choice steps (one bid poll plus 3 plays). 27 rounds is within the 40 limit.
changes.fixes: Too long and too large: 10 hands of growing size means 55 tricks, and with up to 8 players each trick needs more than the 4 choice steps allowed per round.

changes.what: Use a 25-card deck: Green 1-7, Yellow 1-7, Black 1-5, 2 Pirates, 2 Escapes, 1 Mermaid, 1 Skull King. Drop Scary Mary and the second Mermaid.
changes.why: This keeps every type of interaction (following suit, black trump, escapes, the pirate/mermaid/king triangle) with a deck small enough to deal in one random draw. 9 of 25 cards are dealt, so the unseen remainder still creates uncertainty.
changes.fixes: The 70-card deck with many special cards inflates the dealing and resolution steps beyond what the engine builds reliably.

changes.why: This removes the extra declaration choice.
changes.fixes: Scary Mary needs an extra declaration choice when played, which adds a choice step for little strategic value.

changes.what: Flat bid scoring: an exact bid of k (k at least 1) scores 20k; an exact zero bid scores 20; a missed zero bid scores -20; any other miss scores -10 per trick of difference. Bonuses (+30 per Pirate captured by the Skull King, +40 for a Mermaid capturing the Skull King) count only if the bid was exact.
changes.why: The zero bid is now worth the same as bid 1. It is chosen for weak hands, not as a late-game jackpot. All four bids are live options for a 3-card hand.
changes.fixes: The zero-bid payoff (hand number x 10) grows with hand number rather than with difficulty, which distorts late-hand bidding.

changes.what: Rotate the first leader of each hand among the 3 seats. 9 hands means each seat leads first exactly 3 times.
changes.fixes: With growing hand sizes and an uneven count of hands per seat, the first-leader seat is not equalised.

changes.what: The engine offers each player only their legal cards when they play.
changes.why: This keeps the game playable without a judge and prevents rule-breaking moves.
changes.fixes: Too long and too large: 10 hands of growing size means 55 tricks, and with up to 8 players each trick needs more than the 4 choice steps allowed per round.

keeps: Simultaneous exact-trick bidding after seeing your hand, with big rewards for hitting the bid and penalties for missing it.
Must-follow-suit trick play with Black as permanent trump over the colours.
The special-card triangle: Pirate beats Mermaid, Skull King beats Pirate, Mermaid beats Skull King, and Escapes always lose.
Capture bonuses for the Skull King taking Pirates and a Mermaid taking the Skull King.
Several hands with a highest-total winner, in which setting opponents' bids matters as much as making your own.

recommendation.reason: The core of exact-bid trick-taking with hidden hands is strongly reasoning-dependent. It compresses into 3 players, 3-card hands and one trick per round within the limits.

variation.name: Skull King: Three-Card Raids
variation.summary: A compact 3-player Skull King. Over 9 hands of 3 cards each, players simultaneously bid how many of the 3 tricks they will win. They then play tricks with suits, black trump, Escapes, Pirates, a Mermaid and the Skull King, scoring for exact bids and bonus captures.
variation.rules:
PLAYERS AND DECK. 3 players, seats 1, 2 and 3. The deck has 25 cards: Green 1-7 (7 cards), Yellow 1-7 (7 cards), Black 1-5 (5 cards), 2 Pirates, 2 Escapes, 1 Mermaid and 1 Skull King. Green, Yellow and Black are the suited cards. Pirates, Escapes, the Mermaid and the Skull King are special cards.

STRUCTURE. The game has 9 hands of 3 tricks each, so 27 rounds; each round is one trick. Each player's score starts at 0.

START OF EACH HAND (first trick of the hand only). Shuffle all 25 cards and deal 3 to each player, face down. Each player sees only their own cards. The other 16 cards are set aside unseen. All players then bid at the same moment, each secretly choosing a whole number from 0 to 3: the number of tricks they will win this hand. All bids are then revealed to everyone. The first leader of hand h is seat ((h-1) mod 3) + 1, so hands 1, 4 and 7 are led by seat 1, hands 2, 5 and 8 by seat 2, and hands 3, 6 and 9 by seat 3.

PLAYING A TRICK. The leader plays one card face up, then the next seat clockwise (1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 1), then the third player.
- Lead suit: the suit of the first suited card played in the trick. If special cards are played before any suited card, the lead suit is set by the first suited card that follows. If no suited card is played, there is no lead suit.
- Following: once a lead suit exists, a player who holds a card of that suit must play either a card of that suit or a special card. A player with no card of that suit may play any card. Special cards may always be played.
- The engine offers each player only the cards they may legally play.

WINNING A TRICK. Check these in order:
(1) If the trick contains both the Skull King and the Mermaid, the Mermaid wins.
(2) Otherwise, if it contains the Skull King, the Skull King wins.
(3) Otherwise, if it contains a Pirate, the first Pirate played wins.
(4) Otherwise, if it contains the Mermaid, the Mermaid wins.
(5) Otherwise, if it contains any Black card, the highest Black card wins.
(6) Otherwise, if there is a lead suit, the highest card of the lead suit wins.
(7) Otherwise (all Escapes), the first card played wins.

The player who played the winning card wins the trick, adds 1 to their trick count for this hand and leads the next trick of the hand. Capture bonuses are recorded for the trick winner: +30 for each Pirate in a trick won by the Skull King, and +40 if the Mermaid wins a trick containing the Skull King. The winner, the cards played and any bonus are announced to everyone.

END OF EACH HAND (after the third trick). Each player scores:
- Exact bid of 1, 2 or 3: +20 per trick bid, plus all capture bonuses they recorded this hand.
- Exact bid of 0: +20, plus any capture bonuses they recorded this hand (normally none).
- Missed bid of 0: -20, and bonuses are lost.
- Missed bid of 1, 2 or 3: -10 per trick of difference between bid and tricks won, and bonuses are lost.

Scores are announced. Trick counts and bonuses reset to 0 for the next hand.

END OF GAME. After hand 9 (round 27), the game ends.
variation.objective: After 9 hands the player with the highest total score wins. If two or three players tie for the highest total, the game is a draw among the tied players.
variation.expected_effect: Each hand becomes a tight puzzle. Players bid from 3 cards and the public bids of rivals. They then play to land exactly on their own bid while using card order, trumps and Escapes to force rivals over or under theirs. With only 9 of 25 cards dealt, players must infer who holds the Skull King, the Mermaid or a high Black from bids (a bid of 2 or 3 signals strength) and from the cards already played. Deal luck affects bonuses but is averaged over 9 hands, and the exact-bid rule rewards accurate judgement whatever the cards. Simple policies lose. Always bidding 0 gets set by opponents who lead so as to force it to win. Always bidding 3 almost never comes in exact. Always bidding 1 and playing randomly misses often against players who steer tricks. Seat edge is removed by the rotating first lead (3 times per seat). There is no cooperation to unravel, and trailing players in the final hands have a real reason to take risky bids. Talk is deliberately left out. With one winner, players do disagree, but the public simultaneous bids already serve as signals players can test against later play. Free talk would add unenforceable claims about hands at the cost of extra steps, and nothing to agree on that would change the trick play.

balanced.evidence: Hit payoffs: bid 0 = +20, bid 1 = +20, bid 2 = +40, bid 3 = +60, plus bonuses on a hit. Miss payoffs: bid 0 = -20; bid k>0 = -10 per trick of difference. With 3 players and 3 tricks, each player averages 1 trick per hand. ALWAYS BID 1: this hits only when the player takes exactly 1 trick, roughly 40-50% of hands without planning. EV is about 0.45*20 - 0.55*12, so about +3 per hand. A sensible bidder who counts high cards (Skull King, Mermaid, Pirates, high Black) and plays to make the bid hits about 60-70% of hands, often at 40. EV is about +15 to +25 per hand. Over 9 hands the always-1 policy trails by about 100 points and loses to sensible play almost always. Against random play (random bid, random legal card, hit rate about 25-30%, EV near 0 or negative) always-1 usually wins but sometimes loses, so it is not a never-lose policy. ALWAYS BID 3 (highest): it needs all 3 tricks (under 10% of hands) and usually misses by 2 for -20. EV is about -15 per hand, so it loses to everyone. ALWAYS BID 0: it hits only when the player wins nothing. A naive ducker holding a Pirate, Skull King or Mermaid, or forced to follow with a high card, misses often (about 50%) and pays -20, so EV is about 0. It loses to sensible play. ALWAYS PLAY FIRST/LAST LEGAL CARD with a sensible bid: this loses control of trick counts and hits far less often than deliberate play. No card or bid is strictly best: the Skull King loses to the Mermaid, the Mermaid loses to a Pirate, and Escapes are good only when ducking. Winner rule: in no thoughtless policy does the player avoid losing against every opponent behaviour. Seats: hand openers rotate (seat 1 opens hands 1, 4, 7; seat 2 opens 2, 5, 8; seat 3 opens 3, 6, 9). Bids are simultaneous, and every seat gets equal lead and last-to-play positions over the game. There is no seat edge, and all three players can realistically win. There is no 'cooperation' label whose numbers could contradict it.

playable.evidence: Deck and structure: 7+7+5+2+2+1+1 = 25 cards. 9 hands × 3 tricks = 27 rounds, so the game is finite. The deal happens only on trick 1 of a hand (a `when` step), giving 1 random draw per round. Choice steps: the bid poll plus 3 card plays makes 4 on the first trick of a hand and 3 on the others, within the limit of 4. Attributes: score×3 + tricks×3 + bid×3 + bonus×3 + leader = 13, within 20. Hidden elements: private hands and the unseen set-aside cards make 2. Rounds: 27, within 40. Rules are complete: lead suit when specials come first, the follow rule, and a 7-step precedence order where Mermaid beats Black because rule 4 comes before rule 5. The case 'only specials and Black' is covered because Black is suited and so sets the lead suit. Ties within a suit are impossible. The trick winner leads the next trick. Scoring covers every hit and miss case, and the winner is decided by arithmetic on the totals with ties drawn. Rule (7) can never trigger, since there are only 2 Escapes among 3 players, but it is harmless. Legal-card filtering and trick resolution are arithmetic or referee-checkable rule checks. 12 steps is tight but plausible. No board, clock, trading or binding agreements are needed. Three players but no talk: this is sensible. Bids are revealed publicly and every card is played face up, so players reason from that public information rather than guessing. Cheap talk about intentions in a trick-taking game would only add words. Simultaneous bidding is a poll, which is correct. The game is not a repeated cooperation game, so the late-round betrayal test does not apply.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence: Chance: the 3-card deal decides whether a player can bid 2-3 (40-60 points) or only 0-1 (20 points). Over 9 deals this evens out partly. I estimate 35-45% of the result is card luck. Skill drives the rest. Bid estimation must account for 16 unseen cards and how strong a card is given 6 opposing cards. The revealed bids show where the specials likely sit; for example, an opponent bidding 3 likely holds the Skull King or Pirates. Card play involves ducking with Escapes or low cards, dumping specials, and spoiling an opponent's exact bid by forcing them to take or lose a trick. The precedence order and capture bonuses reward timing, such as holding the Mermaid for the Skull King. If all players play well, hit rates rise for everyone. The winner then depends on deal strength plus small edges in reading and spoiling. Deals add variety but do not alone decide outcomes, because a spoiled bid swings 30-40 points. A careful reasoner clearly beats a naive or random bidder: about +15-25 versus about 0-3 per hand, as computed above.
